no untoward events.

the puncture site.

remained intact.

1. L4 Kyphoplasty, uni-pedicular approach for pathological compression 
fracture

DATE OF PROCEDURE: 3/27/25

SURGEON:
Branden John Cord, MD, PhD

RESIDENT:
Cody Key, MD
Clayton Gerndt, MD

SEDATION:
General Anesthesia


COMPLICATIONS:
None.

CLINICAL HISTORY:
80yF h/o of polio and chronic low back pain w/ known superior end-plate 
fractures of L4/L5 dating back to 2020 who initially presented on 3/13/25 
with acute on chronic LBP s/p GLF. At that time she was found to have an 
acute on chronic L4/5 compression fracture. She was discharged with TLSO 
brace for comfort, PCP follow up, and DEXA outpatient. She unfortunately 
continued to have uncontrollable back pain despite pain medication and 
minimal ambulation due to the pain. She is not able to perform her 
activities of daily living. There is pain to palpation overlying the 
fracture site.

I have recommended an L4 balloon kyphoplasty.

The risks/benefits were discussed with the patient and/or family including 
but not limited to non-resolution of pain, worsened pain, bleeding, 
infection, progression of compression fracture, adjacent level fractures, 
vascular cement embolization, pulmonary embolism, cement extravasation 
with compression of nerve roots or spinal cord, puncture of other 
structures with resulting injury, myocardial infarction, and radiation 
injury. All questions asked were answered. Consent signed and in the 
chart.

TECHNIQUE AND FINDINGS:
The patient was positioned prone on the angiography table and the skin 
prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. Antibiotics were 
administered prior to skin incision.

The target vertebra was carefully identified and positioned under biplane 
fluoroscopy. 10cc lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin at the puncture 
site and deepened with a spinal needle to the periosteum overlying the 
pedicle. A 10G kyphoplasty cannula was introduced into the target 
vertebral body via the pedicle. A curved cannula with stylet was advanced 
with a mallet and positioned across the midline of the vertebral body.

A 15-mm kyphoplasty balloon tamp was positioned through the cannula into 
the body. The balloon achieved a successful expansion. Bone cement was 
prepared and injected into the vertebral body through the cannula. When 
the PMMA bone cement was polymerized, the needle was removed.

This procedure was repeated for all treated levels (L4).

A good fill was achieved in L4.

At the termination of the procedure, the skin was cleaned, and a dressing 
applied.

There were no apparent periprocedural complications.

TARGET LEVELS:L4

SUMMARY:
Successful balloon kyphoplasty for pathological compression fracture 
(osteoporotic lesion) at the L4 level, uni-pedicular approach.

84yF h/o osteoporosis, s/p MVC in 2018 with severe underlying back pain. 
She improved with steroid injections. She had a significant fall in 2/2024 
with new severe back pain. Imaging in April of 2024 demonstrated L2 and L3 
compression fractures. She underwent conservative therapy. She had a flair 
of pain in January 2025. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a new T12 
fracture. She again underwent conservative therapy with a brace and pain 
medication and PT. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrates a T12, L2, and L3 
pathological compression fractures. The T12 and L2 vertebral bodies have 
significant edema on MRI, the L3 has mild edema. The pain is limiting her 
activities of daily living.

I have recommended a percutaneous placement of Spine Jack device with 
adjunctive cement augmentation at the T12 and L2 level(s) for fracture 
stabilization and height restoration.

The risks/benefits were discussed with the patient/family including but 
not limited to non-resolution of pain, worsened pain, bleeding, infection, 
progression of compression fracture, device migration, adjacent level 
fractures, vascular cement embolization, pulmonary embolism, cement 
extravasation with compression of nerve roots or spinal cord, puncture of 
other structures with resulting injury, myocardial infarction, and 
radiation injury. All questions asked were answered. Consent signed and in 
the chart.

TECHNIQUE AND FINDINGS:
The patient was positioned prone on the fluoroscopy table and the skin 
prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. Antibiotics were 
administered prior to skin incision.

The target vertebra was carefully identified and positioned under biplane 
fluoroscopy. 10cc lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin at the puncture 
site and deepened with a spinal needle to the periosteum overlying the 
left pedicle. Under fluoroscopic guidance, an access cannula was inserted 
through the bilateral pedicles. K-wires were then advanced with a mallet 
to the anterior wall of the vertebral body. The cannula were removed 
leaving the K-wires in place. On one side a reamer was advanced down the 
K-wire and then removed. A template was then placed to ensure proper size 
of the cavity. This was removed and an access cannula was placed with 
clear template. On the contralateral side, similar steps were taken.

Bilaterally, Spine Jack devices were advanced into the vertebral body. 
They were then incrementally expanded simultaneously under real-time 
fluoroscopy until optimal height restoration achieved.

Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) cement was injected into the vertebral body 
through the spine jack delivery system bilaterally. Cement flow was 
carefully monitored under fluoroscopy to ensure even distribution and 
avoid extravasation into surrounding structures.

The delivery system and spine jack device were then removed, and final 
fluoroscopic images confirmed satisfactory cement placement and vertebral 
stabilization.

At the termination of the procedure, the skin was cleaned, and a dressing 
applied. There were no immediate complications identified. Anesthesia was 
reversed and the patient extubated and transferred to the PACU. There were 
no apparent periprocedural complications.

TARGET LEVEL: T12 and L2

SUMMARY:
Successful Spine Jack device placement with adjunctive cement augmentation 
for fracture stabilization and height restoration of T12 and L2 
pathological compression fractures.

VERTEBRAL ARTERY, high-magnification views, with different projections

There is a small neck residual

Follow up cerebral angiogram at June 2025, and December 2025 to ensure

DATE: 9/17/2021 12:46 PM.

PROCEDURE: CT guided lung biopsy and right chest wall biopsy.

HISTORY: Concern for lung cancer such as pulmonary adenocarcinoma versus tuberculosis

DOCUMENTATION: Informed consent was obtained and a procedural pause was performed to confirm the identity of the patient as well as the intended procedure and operative site. Conscious sedation was required throughout the procedure.

SEDATION START TIME: 1017.
SEDATION END TIME: 1135.
PROCEDURE TIME: 68 minutes.

ATTENDING PRESENCE: Dr. Brian Goldner, the attending physician, was present and actively participated in all aspects of the procedure. Dr. Cody Key (resident) assisted.

CONTRAST: None.

TECHNIQUE: The skin over the right anterior chest wall was sterilely prepped, draped, and infiltrated with 1% lidocaine. Computed tomography was used to locate the right upper lobe pulmonary mass and the right anterior chest wall axillary lymph node.
Using a Seldinger trocar technique, a 20-gauge Chiba FNA needle was placed into the target right axillary lymph node, which is noted to be FDG avid on recent PET/CT. Unfortunately, because of excessive metallic streak artifact caused by the trocar, visualization of the target lymph node was limited. In addition, cytopathology was unavailable to assess samples at time of acquisition. As such, 2 FNA passes were obtained with little to no tissue observed and the needles were rinsed with formalin and disposed. A single 20-gauge 1 cm core biopsy was obtained and placed in formalin.
Next, attention was turned to the right upper lobe peripheral mass. This mass was localized using CT guidance and a trocar was placed along the anterior lateral aspect of the mass.
The nodule was accessed with a 19G thin walled outer needle. No needle aspirations were performed due to the unavailability of cytopathology. We then proceeded to collect 6 20-gauge core samples with 1 cm length each. A post biopsy CT did not demonstrate pneumothorax. While preparing to remove the patient from the table a sucking/wheezing sound was heard, and repeat CT fluoroscopy images were obtained to confirm no pneumothorax present. 5cc of autologous blood was used to close the needle tract at the lung periphery. The needle was then withdrawn. The patient tolerated the procedure well. No immediate complications were encountered.

FINDINGS: CT demonstrates peripheral right upper lobe mass concerning for neoplasm. Previous exam of 8/20/2019 demonstrated subpleural groundglass/consolidation within the tibia, rapidly evolved since then and notably FDG avid. The procedural images show the needle within the peripheral lateral aspect of the right upper lobe mass.

There is a right mediastinal soft tissue density nodule located between the aortic root and SVC measuring 25 Hounsfield units in density and 30 x 20 x 16 mm mm. By comparison, this lesion measured 29 x 19 x 10 mm when measured in similar fashion on exam of 8/20/2019, although demonstrates clearly increased bulging convex borders.

IMPRESSION:

Uneventful right upper lobe CT guided pulmonary mass biopsy. Samples sent for pathologic analysis.

Attempted FDG avid right axillary lymph node biopsy, samples were difficult to obtain due to streak artifact obscuring the target lymph node and unavailability of cytopathology. It is considered less likely that this tissue sampling was successful but FDG avid right axillary lymph node remains concerning for possible right chest wall invasion.

Enlarged since 2019 right mediastinal nodule located between the SVC and aortic root. This is an atypical location for a lymph node. This lesion was noted to be quite FDG avid and is concerning for a malignant. Differential considerations include pleural deposit from the same process in the right upper lobe versus possible thymoma.

Post-procedure diagnosis: Same
Indication: Port no longer needed
Additional clinical history: None

Adverse events: Silicone catheter of the port snapped at the venotomy during gentle traction to remove it from the subcutaneous tissues due to its embedded, scarred in state. 

IMPRESSION:
1. Removal of the left port reservoir and subcutaneous silicone line. 
2. Removal of the intravascular silicone line in the SVC via snaring. 
3. There is a retained fragment of the silicone line in the remnant of the left brachiocephalic and subclavian veins. This fragment is mostly scarred into the wall of the vessels and cannot be removed safely from an endovascular approach.  

Plan:
Please re-consult interventional radiology if new port placement is desired. 

The catheter fragment in the remnant of the brachiocephalic and subclavian veins is mostly scarred into the wall of the vessels. These veins are diseased due to the port being in for so long and no endovascular approach to removal is possible safely. However, as the vessels are already diseased and the catheter is mostly scarred into the wall rather than in the lumen, leaving this catheter fragment in poses negligible additional risk and a surgical removal would likely pose more risk. 
_______________________________________________________________

PROCEDURE SUMMARY:
- Venous port removal
- Additional procedure(s): Snaring of retained intravascular port catheter

Pre-procedure
Consent: Informed consent for the procedure including risks, benefits and alternatives was obtained and time-out was performed prior to the procedure.
Preparation (MIPS): The site was prepared and draped using all elements of maximal sterile barrier technique including sterile gloves, sterile gown, cap, mask, large sterile sheet, sterile ultrasound probe cover, hand hygiene and cutaneous antisepsis with 2% chlorhexidine.
Medical reason for site preparation exception (MIPS): Not applicable

Anesthesia/sedation
Level of anesthesia/sedation: Moderate sedation (conscious sedation)
Anesthesia/sedation administered by: Independent trained observer under attending supervision with continuous monitoring of the patient’s level of consciousness and physiologic status
Total intra-service sedation time (minutes): 246

Port removal
Local anesthesia was administered. Through a small incision, the port was dissected free and the port and attached catheter were attempted to be removed in their entirety. However, the port catheter appeared embedded and scarred in at the venotomy. The catheter was silicone material and any amount of traction would stretch it out. Despite vigorous attempts to attempt to dissect the tissues away near the venotomy, the port's initial subclavian access (surgically placed) prevented percutaneous access to the venotomy without larger cut-down as it was posterior to the clavicle. As such, even with gentle traction, the catheter could not be completely freed from the venotomy and ultimately snapped away at that point. The port and subcutaneous portion of the catheter were then  discarded.

Closure
The port pocket incision was closed.
Incision closure technique: Absorbable suture and tissue adhesive

Access
Local anesthesia was administered. The vessel was sonographically evaluated and determined to be patent. Real time ultrasound was used to visualize needle entry into the vessel and a permanent image was stored. A 5 Fr sheath was placed, which was then upsized to a 9 Fr sheath and then a 16 Fr sheath.
Vein accessed: Right common femoral vein
Access technique: Micropuncture set with 21 gauge needle

Venography
Venography of the left brachiocephalic vein was performed initially to assess the patency and health of the vein and to evaluate the intravascular position of the retained catheter fragment. A Vert catheter and glidewire were used to select the brachiocephalic vein.
Catheter tip position for venography: Left brachiocephalic-subclavian vein
Findings: Diseased brachiocephalic vein, with scarring of the vessel noted. The subclavian vein appears chronically occluded with surrounding collaterals seen. Retained catheter fragment appears to be embedded in the wall of the brachiocephalic vein, and becomes truly intravascular again at the SVC-brachiocephalic vein confluence.  

Retrieval
Initially, a 9 Fr sheath was advanced into the right atrium. Lunderquist wire was placed in the left brachiocephalic vein. An EnSnare device was then used to snare the tip of the port catheter. However, the catheter could not be freed from the scar tissue in the brachiocephalic vein and simply stretched out as it was being pulled due to its silicone nature. An attempt was made to oversheath the catheter in the brachiocephalic vein but the sheath could not be advanced past the confluence with the SVC due to the diseased nature of the vessel. 

A decision was made to upsize the sheath to a 16 Fr and try again to snare the catheter and potentially oversheath the scarred portion by inflating 6 and 7 mm balloons and with deflation, advancing the sheath into the brachiocephalic vein. However, this was not successful despite multiple attempts as it appeared that the catheter would buckle away at the confluence with the sheath movement since it was embedded in the wall of the vessel.

It was decided at that point that the risk of potentially using forceps or other advanced mechanisms of retrieval would outweigh the benefits of removing this already embedded and scarred in catheter fragment, especially since the catheter was located in the mediastinum and near the great vessels. A decision was made to "snap off" and retrieve the remaining intravascular portion in the SVC and right atrium. Another snare was used to march up the catheter and grab the intravascular portion at the confluence of the left brachiocephalic vein and SVC. With the other snare holding the tip and this second snare grabbing the proximal intravascular portion, the catheter was pulled on until it snapped and then removed from the sheath and body intact. 

All that remained after this was the scarred in catheter in the remnant left brachiocephalic and subclavian veins. 

Post-retrieval venography
Post-retrieval venography of the left brachiocephalic vein and SVC was performed.
Findings: Similar diseased appearance of the brachiocephalic and subclavian veins with numerous central collaterals seen. SVC appears patent. No extravasation. 

Closure
The sheath was removed and hemostasis was achieved with manual compression. A sterile dressing was applied.

facilitate neck extension and head turning to the contralateral side. A

the carotid bifurcation was also marked confirming greater than 5cm of 
disease free CCA required for safe insertion of the TCAR sheath. The neck, 
upper chest, and right groin were prepped and draped in standard fashion. 
IV antibiotics were administered prior to skin incision. Neuromonitoring 
baselines were established using EEG and SSEPs. 
  
An 8F venous sheath was inserted using a micropuncture technique over an 
035 wire into the right common femoral vein.
 
A transverse incision was infiltrated with 1% lidocaine and epinephrine 
(1:100,000) approximately 1-cm above the medial clavicle (6 cc). The 
initial incision was made with a #10 blade. The platysma was divided. 
Sharp and blunt dissection allowed us to identify the two heads of the 
sternocleidomastoid muscle. Further dissection in this triangular space 
revealed the internal jugular vein (IJV). It was skeletonized along its 
course. The IJV was reflected laterally to expose the LEFT common carotid 
artery (CCA). The CCA was skeletonized along its most proximal course and 
an umbilical tape wrapped around the vessel to provide proximal control. 
Care was taken not to include the vagus nerve. The IJV was retracted 
laterally. The common carotid artery was placed on mild tension and 
retracted out of the wound using the umbilical tape and secured to the 
drape using a snap instrument. A "U-stitch" was placed in the common 
carotid artery (6-0 Prolene). At this time, the patient was heparinized 
with a goal ACT > 250 seconds. 
 
A micropuncture needle (21G) was slowly advanced through the anterior wall 
of the common carotid artery (via a separate stab incision in the skin). 
Arterial blood flow was documented. A microguidewire (0.018") was inserted 
3-cm into the common carotid artery and a microsheath (4F) advanced 2-3-cm 
inside the artery. The inner dilator and microguidewire were removed. 
Selective injection and angiography of the LEFT COMMON CAROTID ARTERY 
confirmed proper positioning inside the vessel without evidence of 
dissection or injury. Under roadmap guidance, an 0.035" ENROUTE J-wire was 
positioned in the distal common carotid artery and the ENROUTE 
Transcarotid Arterial Sheath successfully inserted into the common carotid 
artery.
 
The sheath was secured at two points using 2-0 silk suture to the 
surrounding skin. Selective injection and angiography of the LEFT COMMON 
CAROTID ARTERY was performed (oblique planes). Note was made of a 
high-grade stenosis (greater than 70%) at the carotid bifurcation. The 
Flow Line and Controller were prepped and connected to the venous sheath 
establishing an extracorporeal arteriovenous shunt (high-flow setting). 
The patient was heparinized.  A "TCAR timeout" was performed to ensure 
systolic blood pressure was maintained greater than 160 mm Hg, heart rate 
was greater than 60 bpm, and all endovascular devices were prepped and on 
the table.
 
The common carotid artery was occluded using a carotid clamp. Flow 
reversal was confirmed using a saline bolus in the Venous Flow Line. 
Selective injection and angiography of the LEFT common carotid artery 
confirmed lesion location and the stent landing zone in addition to flow 
reversal in the ICA.
 
The lesion was crossed using an 014 microguidewire (ENROUTE, Silk Road). 
Proper positioning in the ICA was confirmed by bringing the wire into the 
petrous carotid.

Monorail Balloon. Using a standard "pin and pull" technique, an ENROUTE 
Stent (9 x 40-mm) was deployed across the lesion. No post-stent 
angioplasty was performed. A control run confirmed an excellent 
angiographic result, but a small back wall carotid dissection. A second 
stent (ENROUTE 10 x 40-mm) was deployed to cover the dissection. Control 
runs demonstrates excellent coverage of the dissection. The Arterial Flow 
Line stopcock was turned OFF to the patient. The Arterial Flow Line was 
disconnected and the patient auto-transfused the blood from the Flow Line 
back to the patient's venous system and the Venous Flow Line stopcock 
turned OFF to the patient. The Transcarotid Arterial Sheath was removed 
and the puncture site closed with the "U-stitch." There were no changes in 
electrophysiology during the procedure.
 
Excellent hemostasis was achieved. IV Protamine was administered. The 
platysma was closed using 3-0 Vicryl stitches as were the subcutaneous 
tissues. The skin edges were re-approximated using a subcuticular stitch. 
The small stab incision was closed in similar fashion. The wound was 
washed using wet and dry sponges. Appropriate dressings were applied. The 
venous sheath was removed by manual compression.

The patient was found to be in stable neurological condition and 
transferred to the PACU for continued post-operative care. There were no 
apparent peri-procedural complications.

sternocleidomastoid muscle. Further dissection in this triangular space 
revealed the internal jugular vein (IJV). It was skeletonized along its 
course. The IJV was reflected laterally to expose the LEFT common carotid 
artery (CCA). The CCA was skeletonized along its most proximal course and
